caption: Hi! I'm Dr. Smiley. I live inside an app called Interpreter Hub.
My friend Jose made it. He works at Hackensack, and he's not a programmer. He didn't write the code. Claude did.
Here's the trick. Think of Claude as a junior developer: a fast, eager helper who builds whatever you describe.
You're the boss. You bring the idea. Claude does the typing.
Step one. Before any code, ask Claude for a short plan: what the app does, who it's for, and what it will NOT do yet.
That last part matters. Without it, your helper keeps adding things, and nothing gets finished.
Step two. Ask for one small thing at a time.
Step three. Check its work. Ask Claude to test it and show you a screenshot. Don't just take its word for it.
Step four. Tell it what's wrong in plain words: where you tapped, and what happened.
Then do it again. Plan, build, check, fix. That's how a glossary, a quiz and a 3D body ended up in one app.
Try it today: tell Claude your app idea, and ask it to interview you until it can write the plan.
If you keep telling Claude the same thing in every chat, there's a better way.
Put it in your profile. Claude applies your profile instructions to every conversation you have with it.
On claude.ai, tap your initials, then Settings, then Your Claude, then Instructions.
Write it like you'd brief a new coworker. Who you are, what you're working on, and how you want answers.
Here's what Jose wrote. Use plain words, I'm new to this. When there are choices, give me buttons, and tell me your pick. Challenge me. Tell me when my idea is weak.
That last one is the most useful. A helper that always says yes will happily build a bad idea.
Short and clear works best. A few good lines beat a long essay.
Try it today: write five lines about how you want Claude to talk to you.
Your profile is about you. CLAUDE.md is about your project.
To build apps, people use Claude Code, the version of Claude that can open your project's files and change them.
CLAUDE.md is a plain text file that lives in your project. Claude Code reads it at the start of every session.
Think of the note you leave a babysitter. Bedtime is at eight. No candy. Don't open the back door, the dog gets out.
For an app, it says what the app is, where everything lives, the rules, and the mistakes never to repeat.
Here's the Hub's. A map of every file. A rule: never change the version number by hand, a robot does that. And a lesson learned the hard way: hover effects don't work on phones.
When Claude gets something wrong and you work out why, the lesson goes in the file. The next chat already knows it.
To start one, type slash init. Claude looks at your project and writes a first draft. Then you add what it can't see on its own.
Keep it short. Anthropic suggests under two hundred lines. Ours grew much longer. Don't copy that part.
Try it today: open your project in Claude Code, type slash init, and read what it wrote.
Last one: the handoff.
A chat with Claude has a working memory, called its context. It's measured in tokens: little pieces of words.
Everything in the chat goes in. What you said, what Claude read, what it wrote.
Every time you send a message, Claude re-reads the whole chat. So a long chat costs more, and its focus gets fuzzier.
When it gets really full, Claude squeezes the old part into a summary. Anything the summary left out is gone.
So don't wait for that. When a chat gets heavy, or a job is done, ask Claude to write a handoff.
It's one page. What you're working on, where it stands, what's next, and the exact message to paste into a new chat.
Open a new chat and paste it. The new chat reads your note and your CLAUDE.md, and picks up where you left off, with a clean memory.
One more tip. If you've corrected Claude twice and it's still wrong, start fresh with one better message. Anthropic says that works better almost every time.
Try it today: at the end of your next long chat, ask Claude to write a handoff for a new chat.
A profile for you. A rulebook for your project. A handoff for every fresh start. Now go build something.
